newsitem.title: USA: Depressed paper, lumber prices hurt earnings.
newsitem.headline: Depressed paper, lumber prices hurt earnings.

text.p: Overcapacity in the paper industry and declining prices for building products hurt the first-quarter earnings of three forestry companies that reported Monday.
Bowater Inc. and Boise Cascade Corp. reported losses for the quarter, in line with industry expectations, while Louisiana-Pacific Corp. reported a profit only because of a one-time gain.

Bowater, the nation's largest producer of newsprint, said it lost $300,000, or 3 cents a share, compared with a profit of $112.9 million, or $2.53 a share, in the first quarter of 1996. Sales fell to $348.5 million from $468.9 million.
The Greenville, S.C.-based company said paper and pulp products prices appear to be stabilising.
"We appear to be at the bottom of the current market cycle," said Arnold Nemirow, chairman and chief executive officer. "The company's product pricing is improving."
Bowater recently announced price increases for newsprint and coated papers, he said.
Bowater stock fell $1 to $38.75 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Boise Cascade said it lost $15.2 million, or 51 cents a share, on sales of $1.28 billion, vs. a year-ago profit of $25.5 million, or 32 cents a share, on sales of $1.22 bilion.
Boise Cascade also blamed deteriorating paper prices, which averaged 26 percent below a year ago.
The Boise, Idaho-based company said it expects the paper business to strengthen this year, as order backlogs lengthen and paper prices improve.
Boise Cascade stock dropped 50 cents to $29.
Louisiana-Pacific Corp. reported a net profit of $42 million or 39 cents a share in the quarter, but only because of a gain from settlement of a dispute over its supply of federal timber in Alaska.
Without the one-time gain the Portland, Ore., company would have lost $32 million, or 29 cents a share, compared with a loss of $3.6 million, or 3 cents a share in the first quarter of 1996.
Analysts had estimated the company would lose 18 cents a share in the quarter, according to First Call.
Sales fell to $554.6 million from $584.1 million a year earlier.

"The biggest factor in the first quarter's poor performance was the oversupply and resulting price declines in oriented strand board construction panels," said Mark Suwyn, Louisiana-Pacific's chairman and chief executive officer.
He said prices for the engineered lumber product were off 40 percent from mid-1996 levels.

"We believe that overcapacity in the construction panel business will be resolved over time as more demand is generated and the less efficient producers are forced to close their operations," Suwyn said.
Pulp revenues sales also were down but accounted for less than 10 percent of the company's business.
Louisiana-Pacific stock gained 12.5 cents to $18.

Boise Cascade's partly owned office products unit -- Boise Cascade Office Products Corp. -- reported income of $14.9 million, or 24 cents a share, in the first quarter, vs. earnings of $15.6 million, or 25 cents a share, a year earlier. Sales jumped 30 percent to $598.0 million from $461.4 million.
Boise Cascade Office's stock, which trades separately from the parent company's, also rose 25 cents to close at $18.125.
